words.definition: The study of relationships among organisms and between organisms and their environment.

structure.text: The ending -logy names a field of study. Ecology studies organisms in relation to their environment; the word names a discipline, not a single ecosystem.

words.whatItDoes: Ecological investigations relate distributions and interactions to conditions, using observations, comparisons and stated system boundaries.
words.commonConfusion: Ecology is a field of study, not a synonym for environmental protection.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could you investigate whether shade affects where moss grows? Name one measurement and one competing explanation.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: The parts selected for an investigation, separated from their surroundings by a stated boundary.

structure.text: System is the head noun: a set of interacting parts. In open system and closed system, the first word specifies what can cross the boundary.

words.whatItDoes: Choosing the parts and boundary lets you classify changes as internal transfers or exchanges with surroundings.
words.commonConfusion: A visible container is not the only possible boundary; the investigator must state what is included.
words.retrievalPrompt: Define a pond system and give one transfer inside it and one transfer across its boundary.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: A system that exchanges both matter and energy with its surroundings.

structure.text: Open modifies system: matter and energy can cross the chosen boundary. Open refers to exchange, not necessarily a visible opening.

words.whatItDoes: Matter and energy can cross the boundary, so both inputs and outputs belong in its balance.
words.commonConfusion: Open describes exchanges, not whether the system has a lid or looks exposed.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is a pond receiving sunlight and runoff an open system? Identify both kinds of exchange.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: A system that exchanges energy but approximately no matter with its surroundings over the stated interval.

structure.text: Closed modifies system: matter exchange is excluded in the stated model, while energy exchange may continue.

words.whatItDoes: A closed-system model excludes matter crossing the boundary while allowing energy transfers such as light and heat.
words.commonConfusion: Closed is not isolated. Changes of state inside a sealed jar do not necessarily move matter across its boundary.
words.retrievalPrompt: Water evaporates inside a sealed illuminated jar. Does that alone make it open? Explain using the boundary.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: An ideal system that exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings.

structure.text: Isolated is a modifier meaning separated from exchange. An isolated-system model excludes both matter and energy exchange.

words.whatItDoes: The idealized boundary excludes energy as well as matter transfers, allowing internal changes to be studied without external exchanges.
words.commonConfusion: Insulation does not prove perfect isolation; real containers can still transfer some energy.
words.retrievalPrompt: A sealed jar receives light. Why can it be approximately closed but not isolated?
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: The regions of Earth where life occurs.

structure.text: Bio- concerns life; sphere names the Earth-scale region in this compound. It is the region supporting life, not a solid biological shell.

words.whatItDoes: Living organisms interact with air, water and rock across the regions that support life, connecting local ecosystems through matter transfers.
words.commonConfusion: Biosphere is not another name for the atmosphere; life also occurs in water and parts of the ground.
words.retrievalPrompt: Give one example each of life associated with air, water and soil, then connect two through a matter transfer.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: The fraction of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface.

structure.text: Albedo is used as a whole technical noun. An albedo value is a reflected fraction; higher and lower modify that fraction, not surface temperature directly.

words.whatItDoes: It gives the reflected fraction by dividing reflected radiation by incoming radiation under comparable conditions.
words.commonConfusion: A higher reflected fraction need not mean a greater total energy reflection when incoming amounts differ.
words.retrievalPrompt: A surface reflects 240 J of 800 J received. Calculate its albedo and explain what the value means.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: A response that amplifies an initial change.

structure.text: Feedback names a response fed back into a process. Positive specifies reinforcement of the initiating change, not whether the result is desirable.

words.whatItDoes: A returning causal effect reinforces the initial change, which can drive the system farther in the same direction until other limits intervene.
words.commonConfusion: Positive means amplifying, not beneficial. A correlation alone does not establish a feedback loop.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how less reflective cover could amplify warming, naming the returning effect and one condition the explanation assumes.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: An organism that builds organic material using inorganic carbon, with an energy input.

structure.text: Auto- means self. In this nutritional term, troph concerns nourishment: the organism builds organic material from inorganic carbon using an energy source.

words.whatItDoes: It incorporates inorganic carbon into organic material using an energy source, supplying organic matter that can enter food webs.
words.commonConfusion: Autotroph does not mean an organism needs no inputs, and not all autotrophs use light.
words.retrievalPrompt: Two organisms use CO₂ as a carbon source, but only one uses light. Can both be autotrophs? Explain.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: A process that uses light energy to support the production of organic material; oxygenic photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water and releases oxygen.

structure.text: Photo- refers to light; synthesis means putting components together. The compound connects light energy with the synthesis of organic material.

words.whatItDoes: Light-driven reactions support organic-matter production. In the oxygenic pathway considered here, water supplies electrons and oxygen is released.
words.commonConfusion: Plants also respire. Detecting photosynthesis does not show that net oxygen must rise under every condition.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can a photosynthetic organism both release and consume oxygen? Distinguish the processes.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: Production of organic material using energy from chemical reactions rather than light; this lesson considers organisms fixing inorganic carbon.

structure.text: Chemo- refers to chemical processes; synthesis means building a substance. The term contrasts chemical energy sources with light-driven synthesis.

words.whatItDoes: In the examples studied, energy from chemical reactions supports fixation of inorganic carbon into organic matter without light as the energy input.
words.commonConfusion: An organism living in darkness is not necessarily chemosynthetic; it may consume organic matter made elsewhere.
words.retrievalPrompt: What evidence about carbon and energy sources would distinguish a chemosynthetic producer from a consumer in darkness?
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: Cellular reactions that transfer energy available from organic molecules into usable forms, including ATP.

structure.text: Cellular is the adjective from cell. Respiration here names cellular energy-releasing reactions, not simply breathing with lungs.

words.whatItDoes: It transfers some energy available in organic molecules into ATP-linked cellular work; aerobic respiration consumes oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
words.commonConfusion: Respiration is not the same as breathing, and it occurs in producers as well as consumers.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain why oxygen could fall in a closed model containing plants when respiration exceeds oxygen production.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: A conserved physical quantity that can be transferred and transformed; ecological accounts track its inputs, outputs and storage.

structure.text: Energy is the head noun in light energy, chemical energy and thermal energy. The modifier names a form or transfer context; it does not create a different conservation rule.

words.whatItDoes: Energy transfers and transformations support biological processes. Accounting compares inputs, outputs and changes in storage without treating energy as created or destroyed.
words.commonConfusion: Less energy reaching the next trophic level does not mean energy vanished; it may have left the chosen pathway as heat or other transfers.
words.retrievalPrompt: A model receives 1,000 J and reflects 800 J with no transmission. Find the absorbed amount and explain why conservation holds.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: A representation of interconnected feeding relationships in a stated ecological system.

structure.text: Food identifies feeding relationships; web describes many connected pathways rather than one straight chain.

words.whatItDoes: It represents several linked feeding pathways; arrows from food to eater track the direction of transferred matter and chemical energy.
words.commonConfusion: An organism can occupy different trophic positions in different chains within one web.
words.retrievalPrompt: Draw plant → insect → bird and add a bird eating seeds. Explain why the bird now has more than one trophic position.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: An organism that chemically breaks down organic matter, commonly releasing enzymes and absorbing products.

structure.text: Decompose names breakdown; -er names an agent performing a process. A decomposer obtains resources by breaking down organic material.

words.whatItDoes: Enzymatic breakdown of dead organic material makes smaller substances available for uptake and contributes to the return of nutrients to nonliving stores.
words.commonConfusion: Decomposers are not simply one final trophic level; material can reach them from several levels.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why should dead material from both plants and predators connect to decomposers in a food-web model?
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: The receiving trophic level's production divided by source-level production over matching boundaries, usually expressed as a percentage.

structure.text: Transfer names movement between parts of a system; efficiency names the useful-output fraction relative to a specified input.

words.whatItDoes: The ratio compares the receiving level’s production with source-level production over matching area, time and energy units.
words.commonConfusion: Ten percent is not universal. Production divided by ingestion is a different ratio.
words.retrievalPrompt: A source produces 1,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ and the next level produces 80. Calculate transfer efficiency and identify the denominator.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: The substance H₂O; its polarity and hydrogen bonding contribute to properties important to living systems.

structure.text: Water is the substance name; H2O is its chemical formula. The subscript 2 counts hydrogen atoms per molecule, not two kinds of water.

words.whatItDoes: Its molecular properties support dissolving and moving substances, temperature buffering and the cohesion and adhesion important in biological systems.
words.commonConfusion: Cohesion and adhesion describe different interactions; neither means water moves without an energy or pressure context.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain one way water’s interactions with itself differ from its interactions with a suitable solid surface.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: Transfers of water among stores through processes including evaporation, precipitation, infiltration and runoff.

structure.text: Hydro- refers to water; hydrologic is an adjective. Cycle names connected transfers among reservoirs, not one water molecule following a fixed timetable.

words.whatItDoes: Processes move water among atmosphere, surface water, soil, organisms and other stores; a local water budget depends on the chosen boundary and interval.
words.commonConfusion: A cycle does not imply equal local inflow and outflow during every interval.
words.retrievalPrompt: A pond receives 20 units and loses 30 units of water in an interval. Explain its storage change and why the water cycle still operates.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: The chemical element present in carbon dioxide and in the organic compounds of living systems.

structure.text: Carbon is an element name; C is its symbol. Carbon cycle concerns movement of carbon atoms among substances and reservoirs.

words.whatItDoes: Carbon atoms form part of organic compounds and also occur in inorganic stores; photosynthesis and respiration move them between compounds.
words.commonConfusion: Carbon, carbon dioxide and organic carbon compounds are not interchangeable names for the same substance.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace a carbon atom from atmospheric CO₂ into a plant and back to the atmosphere, naming two processes.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: Transfers and chemical transformations of nitrogen among organisms and nonliving stores.

structure.text: Nitrogen specifies the element; cycle names its transfers and transformations. The element is conserved while its chemical form changes.

words.whatItDoes: Fixation, uptake and other transformations redistribute nitrogen among chemical forms and stores, affecting its availability to organisms.
words.commonConfusion: Nitrogen cycling does not mean plants directly use atmospheric N₂ in the same way they take up nitrate.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain why fixation and nitrification are different steps even though both involve nitrogen.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: The mass of living material within a defined system, often measured as dry mass for ecological comparisons.

structure.text: Bio- concerns living material; mass is the measured quantity. Biomass is an amount, whereas productivity includes a time interval.

words.whatItDoes: A standing-biomass measurement estimates living material at a specified time within a defined area or volume.
words.commonConfusion: A biomass stock is not a production rate; rapid turnover can support consumers despite a small standing producer stock.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could a small producer biomass support a larger consumer biomass without creating energy?
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: A comparison of trophic levels using numbers, biomass or energy production, with the quantity and units specified.

structure.text: Ecological connects the representation to organism relationships; pyramid names a layered diagram. Numbers, biomass or energy specify what each layer measures.

words.whatItDoes: It compares specified quantities across trophic levels; the interpretation depends on whether width represents counts, standing biomass or energy production.
words.commonConfusion: An inverted biomass pyramid is not evidence of inverted energy production or a failure of energy conservation.
words.retrievalPrompt: What units and time information would you need before interpreting a pyramid labelled “energy”?
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: A chemical element; molecular oxygen, O₂, is released by oxygenic photosynthesis and used in aerobic respiration.

structure.text: Oxygen is the element name; O2 specifies a molecule containing two oxygen atoms. The formula and the element name are not interchangeable quantities.

words.whatItDoes: Molecular oxygen participates in aerobic respiration and is released by oxygenic photosynthesis; its net amount depends on all relevant sources and sinks.
words.commonConfusion: The oxygen element occurs in many compounds; an oxygen atom in water is not a molecule of O₂.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does finding producers in a model not guarantee that its O₂ concentration will rise?
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: An organism that builds organic matter from inorganic carbon using a source of energy; ecological producers include photosynthetic and chemosynthetic autotrophs.

structure.text: Produce names making something; -er names the agent. In ecology, producer is a nutritional role, not a claim that energy is created.

words.whatItDoes: It supplies newly built organic matter from inorganic carbon, introducing material into feeding pathways using an appropriate energy source.
words.commonConfusion: Producer does not mean only a green plant; chemosynthetic autotrophs can also serve this role.
words.retrievalPrompt: Describe a producer that does not depend on light as its immediate energy source, and identify its carbon input.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: An organism that obtains organic matter by feeding on other organisms or their products; its trophic position depends on the stated feeding pathway.

structure.text: Consume names taking in resources; -er names the agent. The ecological noun concerns obtaining organic material from other organisms.

words.whatItDoes: It obtains organic matter through feeding and transfers some of that matter and energy through the food web.
words.commonConfusion: Consumer does not identify a fixed trophic level; an omnivore’s position depends on the pathway considered.
words.retrievalPrompt: An animal eats both leaves and insects. Explain its trophic position in each pathway.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: The chemical element N, present in amino acids and nucleic acids; its chemical form affects its biological availability.

structure.text: Nitrogen is the element name and N its symbol. N2 names a two-atom molecule; nitrate and ammonium name different nitrogen-containing ions.

words.whatItDoes: Nitrogen atoms are incorporated into amino acids and nucleic acids; organisms need usable chemical forms and appropriate uptake pathways.
words.commonConfusion: Abundant atmospheric nitrogen does not guarantee usable nitrogen for a plant.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can a plant have a limited nitrogen supply while surrounded by air containing N₂?
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: The chemical element P, present in nucleic acids, phospholipids and energy-transfer compounds; plants obtain it principally as phosphate from their surroundings.

structure.text: Phosphorus is an element name, symbol P. Phosphate names an ion containing phosphorus and oxygen; the two names do not identify the same chemical form.

words.whatItDoes: Phosphorus-containing compounds contribute to membranes, nucleic acids and energy transfer; phosphate moves through organisms and nonliving stores.
words.commonConfusion: Elemental phosphorus and phosphate are not the same chemical species.
words.retrievalPrompt: Trace phosphate from soil into a plant and explain one biological use of its phosphorus.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: The chemical element S, found in some amino acids and in nonliving stores; sulfate in soil water is an important plant source.

structure.text: Sulfur is an element name, symbol S. Sulfate and sulfide name different sulfur-containing chemical forms.

words.whatItDoes: Sulfur is incorporated into some amino acids and moves among biological and geological stores in different chemical forms.
words.commonConfusion: A sulfur-containing substance is not necessarily hydrogen sulfide, and smell cannot identify the entire sulfur cycle.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is sulfur taken up as sulfate still part of a sulfur cycle that also includes organic compounds?
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: Attraction among molecules of the same substance; attractions among water molecules contribute to its surface behaviour.

structure.text: Cohesion belongs with cohesive: attraction among like molecules. Compare adhesion, which concerns attraction between different materials.

words.whatItDoes: Attractions among water molecules help maintain connected water surfaces and columns; they contribute to surface tension.
words.commonConfusion: Cohesion concerns like-with-like attraction. Attraction between water and a different surface is adhesion.
words.retrievalPrompt: Water molecules attract neighbouring water molecules in a droplet. Name the interaction and contrast it with attraction to glass.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: Attraction between different substances, such as water and a suitable solid surface.

structure.text: Adhesion belongs with adhesive: attachment between different materials. Compare cohesion among water molecules.

words.whatItDoes: Attraction between water and a suitable different material helps water wet surfaces and contributes, with cohesion, to capillary behaviour.
words.commonConfusion: Adhesion is not the attraction of water molecules to one another, and not every surface is equally wettable.
words.retrievalPrompt: Water climbs partly along the wall of a narrow tube. Identify the interaction with the wall and distinguish it from cohesion.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: Conversion of molecular nitrogen, N₂, into reduced forms that can enter biological nitrogen pathways.

structure.text: Nitrogen names the element; fixation names its conversion from atmospheric N2 into biologically usable compounds, not physical fastening.

words.whatItDoes: It converts relatively unreactive N₂ into reduced nitrogen forms that can become available through biological pathways.
words.commonConfusion: Fixation is not the oxidation of ammonium into nitrate; that is nitrification.
words.retrievalPrompt: A process starts with atmospheric N₂ and produces reduced nitrogen. Which step is this, and how does its input differ from nitrification?
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: Oxidation of ammonium through nitrite to nitrate; this transforms already-fixed nitrogen.

structure.text: The process noun ends in -ification. It names oxidation through ammonium, nitrite and nitrate stages; it is not another name for nitrogen fixation.

words.whatItDoes: Microbial oxidation changes ammonium through nitrite into nitrate, changing the form of already-fixed nitrogen.
words.commonConfusion: Nitrification does not begin with atmospheric N₂ and does not mean adding new nitrogen atoms to the system.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can conversion of ammonium to nitrate alter nitrogen availability without increasing the total number of nitrogen atoms?
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: Microbial reduction of nitrate or nitrite to gaseous nitrogen products under suitable conditions, commonly where oxygen is limited.

structure.text: De- marks removal or reversal in this process name. Denitrification returns nitrogen from nitrate-related forms toward gaseous forms, rather than producing nitrate.

words.whatItDoes: Under suitable conditions, microbial reduction can convert nitrate or nitrite into gaseous nitrogen products, moving nitrogen out of some local soil or water pools.
words.commonConfusion: Denitrification is not nitrogen fixation; the starting forms and direction of transformation differ.
words.retrievalPrompt: Explain how nitrate in water could decrease through denitrification and name a condition relevant to that explanation.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: Nutrient enrichment that can increase production and alter aquatic conditions, including oxygen balance; effects depend on the system.

structure.text: This is a process noun ending in -ication. In this course it names nutrient enrichment and its ecological consequences; distinguish enrichment from any one resulting algal bloom.

words.whatItDoes: Nutrient enrichment can stimulate production; subsequent respiration and decomposition may increase oxygen demand and alter aquatic communities.
words.commonConfusion: An algal increase alone does not quantify oxygen loss, and enrichment does not cause identical effects in every system.
words.retrievalPrompt: Connect nutrient addition to a possible later oxygen decrease, naming the biological steps and one missing measurement.
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending

words.definition: The rate of biological production over a stated area or volume and time; it is not simply the standing amount of biomass.

structure.text: Productive is an adjective; productivity is the corresponding measured process or rate. A time interval distinguishes production rate from standing biomass.

words.whatItDoes: It describes production per unit time within stated spatial boundaries, allowing rates to be compared rather than only standing stocks.
words.commonConfusion: Two systems with the same biomass can have different productivity because their rates of production and turnover differ.
words.retrievalPrompt: What extra measurement is needed to distinguish a biomass measurement from a productivity estimate?
words.reviewStatus: authored-from-existing-course; second scientific review and learner integration pending
